claims.text: Gradient processing can create a heterogeneous microstructure containing both ultrafine and coarse grains.
A heterogeneous gradient microstructure can overcome the conventional strength–ductility trade-off in metals.
Conventional processing produces a homogeneous microstructure with a uniform grain size in the proposed initial alloy.
Controlled severe plastic deformation can produce a spatial transition from ultrafine to coarser grains.
Gradient heat treatment can produce a spatial transition from ultrafine to coarser grains.
Ultrafine grains impart high strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarse grains enhance plasticity and ductility.
Ultrafine-grained regions inhibit dislocation motion and thereby enhance strength.
Coarser-grained regions provide pathways for strain accommodation and thereby enhance ductility.
The combination of ultrafine- and coarse-grained regions creates a synergistic effect that mitigates the strength–ductility trade-off.
Relative to a homogeneous control, the gradient-structured material will have higher yield strength under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading.
Relative to a homogeneous control, the gradient-structured material will have greater uniform elongation under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading.
Increasing strength in a homogeneous, uniform-grained material typically reduces its ductility.
Very high strain rates may limit the benefits of the gradient microstructure by activating additional deformation mechanisms.
Elevated operating temperatures may limit the benefits of the gradient microstructure by activating additional deformation mechanisms.
The quantitative effects of gradient steepness and transition width on strength and ductility are not fully determined.
